title: Earth Science & The Atmosphere
description: Earth's structure, the rock cycle, the atmosphere's evolution, greenhouse effect, climate change, and sustainable resources.

notes.heading: Earth's Structure
notes.body: The Earth is composed of layers: (1) Crust — the thin outer layer (5-70 km thick). Continental crust is thicker and made of granite; oceanic crust is thinner, denser basalt. (2) Mantle — thickest layer (~2900 km), composed of semi-molten rock (magma). Convection currents in the mantle drive plate tectonics. (3) Outer core — liquid iron and nickel, ~2200 km thick. The movement of liquid iron generates Earth's magnetic field. (4) Inner core — solid iron and nickel (despite extreme heat, immense pressure keeps it solid), ~1200 km radius, temperature ~5500°C. The lithosphere (crust + upper rigid mantle) is broken into tectonic plates that float on the semi-molten asthenosphere. Plate movement causes: earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain formation, and continental drift.

illustration.alt: Cross-section of Earth showing the crust, mantle, outer core, inner core, lithosphere, and asthenosphere.
illustration.caption: The lithosphere (crust + rigid upper mantle) floats on the semi-molten asthenosphere below.

notes.heading: The Rock Cycle
notes.body: Rocks are continuously recycled through three main types: (1) Igneous rocks — formed when magma/lava cools and solidifies. Intrusive (cool slowly underground → large crystals, e.g., granite). Extrusive (cool quickly at surface → small crystals, e.g., basalt, obsidian). (2) Sedimentary rocks — formed from compressed layers of sediment (weathered rock fragments, organic matter, mineral deposits). Often contain fossils. Examples: limestone (calcium carbonate from shells), sandstone (compressed sand), shale (compressed clay). (3) Metamorphic rocks — existing rocks changed by extreme heat and/or pressure without melting. Examples: limestone → marble, shale → slate, granite → gneiss. The rock cycle: weathering & erosion → sediment → burial & compaction → sedimentary rock → heat & pressure → metamorphic rock → melting → magma → cooling → igneous rock. Weathering: physical (freeze-thaw, exfoliation), chemical (acid rain dissolving limestone), biological (root action).

illustration.alt: Rock cycle diagram linking igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks with arrows showing weathering, heat, pressure, melting, and cooling.
illustration.caption: Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks transform into one another through weathering, heat, pressure, and melting.

notes.heading: Evolution of the Atmosphere
notes.body: Earth's atmosphere has changed dramatically over 4.6 billion years: Phase 1 (first billion years): Intense volcanic activity released gases — mainly CO₂, water vapour, and nitrogen. Small amounts of methane (CH₄) and ammonia (NH₃). Virtually NO oxygen. Phase 2: As Earth cooled, water vapour condensed → oceans formed. CO₂ dissolved in oceans → formed carbonate precipitates → limestone rock (locked away carbon). Algae and early plants evolved photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Oxygen levels gradually increased. Phase 3 (last ~400 million years): Oxygen reached levels supporting complex life. The ozone layer (O₃) formed, blocking harmful UV radiation and allowing life to colonise land. Today's atmosphere: Nitrogen ~78%, Oxygen ~21%, Argon ~0.9%, CO₂ ~0.04% (and rising), trace gases. Evidence for early atmosphere: ancient rocks, fossil records, gas trapped in ice cores.

illustration.alt: Three-phase timeline showing the evolution of Earth's atmosphere from volcanic gases to oxygen-rich air.
illustration.caption: Volcanic gases dominated early Earth; cooling oceans and photosynthesis gradually created today's oxygen-rich atmosphere.

notes.heading: Greenhouse Effect and Climate Change
notes.body: The greenhouse effect is a NATURAL process that keeps Earth warm enough for life. How it works: (1) Short-wavelength solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. (2) Earth re-radiates longer-wavelength infrared (heat) radiation back. (3) Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O vapour) absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions — including back to Earth. Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be about −18°C instead of +15°C. The ENHANCED greenhouse effect (global warming): human activities have dramatically increased greenhouse gas concentrations — burning fossil fuels (CO₂), agriculture (CH₄ from cattle, rice paddies), deforestation (fewer trees to absorb CO₂), landfills (CH₄). Evidence for climate change: rising global temperatures (~1.2°C since pre-industrial era), melting ice caps and glaciers, sea level rise, more frequent extreme weather events, changing migration patterns and growing seasons.

illustration.alt: Diagram of the greenhouse effect showing solar radiation entering the atmosphere and heat being trapped by greenhouse gases.
illustration.caption: Greenhouse gases trap infrared heat; human activities enhance this effect, causing global warming.

notes.heading: The Carbon Cycle and Carbon Footprint
notes.body: The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, organisms, oceans, and rocks. Key processes: (1) Photosynthesis — removes CO₂ from air. (2) Respiration — releases CO₂. (3) Feeding — carbon moves through food chains. (4) Decomposition — decomposers release CO₂ from dead matter. (5) Combustion — burning fossil fuels releases stored carbon as CO₂. (6) Dissolving — CO₂ dissolves in oceans (causing ocean acidification). (7) Sedimentation — marine organisms' shells (CaCO₃) sink to the ocean floor → limestone rock — long-term carbon storage. A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an individual, organisation, or product. Reducing carbon footprint: use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), improve energy efficiency, reduce meat consumption (livestock produce methane), use public transport/EVs, plant trees, recycle and reduce waste.

illustration.alt: Carbon cycle diagram showing carbon moving between the atmosphere, plants, animals, oceans, fossil fuels, and limestone rock.
illustration.caption: Carbon cycles through the atmosphere, living things, oceans, and rocks; burning fossil fuels adds extra CO₂.

notes.heading: Atmospheric Pollution
notes.body: Burning fossil fuels produces pollutants: (1) Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — greenhouse gas, climate change. (2) Carbon monoxide (CO) — toxic gas from incomplete combustion; binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport. (3) Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) — from sulfur impurities in coal/oil; causes acid rain (SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ → H₂SO₄). Acid rain damages forests, acidifies lakes (kills aquatic life), erodes stone buildings. (4) Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) — formed when N₂ and O₂ react at high temperatures in car engines. Cause acid rain AND photochemical smog. (5) Particulates (soot, PM2.5) — tiny particles causing respiratory problems, lung cancer. Solutions: catalytic converters (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂), flue gas desulfurisation in power stations, switching to renewable energy, electric vehicles.

illustration.alt: Diagram of atmospheric pollution showing pollutants from power stations and cars, and a catalytic converter reaction.
illustration.caption: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, CO, SO₂, NOₓ and particulates; catalytic converters help reduce some pollutants.

notes.heading: Sustainable Resources and Potable Water
notes.body: Potable water is water safe to drink — it is NOT the same as pure water (no dissolved substances). Potable water contains dissolved minerals and has low levels of microbes. Producing potable water from fresh water: (1) Choose a good source (river, reservoir, groundwater). (2) Pass through screens to remove large debris. (3) Sedimentation — allow particles to settle. (4) Filtration through sand and gravel beds — removes smaller suspended solids. (5) Sterilisation — chlorine gas (kills bacteria/viruses), ozone, or UV light. Desalination (from seawater): distillation or reverse osmosis — energy-intensive and expensive; used in arid regions (e.g., Middle East). Waste water treatment: (1) Screening, (2) Primary sedimentation, (3) Biological treatment (aerobic bacteria digest organic matter), (4) Final sedimentation, (5) Sterilisation before release into rivers. Finite resources: fossil fuels, metal ores, minerals. Sustainable alternatives: renewable energy, metal recycling, green chemistry (designing products/processes that reduce hazardous substances).

illustration.alt: Flow diagram showing the stages of potable water treatment: screening, sedimentation, filtration, and sterilisation.
illustration.caption: Fresh water is screened, sedimented, filtered, and sterilised to make it safe to drink.

flashcards.definition: Rock formed from cooled and solidified magma/lava. Intrusive (slow cooling → large crystals, e.g., granite). Extrusive (fast cooling → small crystals, e.g., basalt).
flashcards.example: Granite (intrusive — visible crystals); obsidian (extrusive — glassy, no visible crystals).

flashcards.definition: Rock formed from compressed layers of sediment (weathered material, organic matter). Often contains fossils. Porous.
flashcards.example: Limestone (CaCO₃ from shells/coral), sandstone (compressed sand grains), shale (compressed clay).

flashcards.definition: Rock changed by extreme heat and/or pressure without melting. Original minerals recrystallise in new arrangements.
flashcards.example: Limestone → marble. Shale → slate. Granite → gneiss.

flashcards.definition: Natural warming process: greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O) trap infrared radiation in the atmosphere, keeping Earth ~33°C warmer.
flashcards.example: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth would be a frozen −18°C — life as we know it could not exist.

flashcards.definition: Human activities (fossil fuel burning, deforestation, agriculture) increase greenhouse gas concentrations, trapping more heat → global warming.
flashcards.example: CO₂ levels have risen from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm today.

flashcards.definition: Rainwater acidified by dissolved SO₂ and NOₓ from burning fossil fuels. Damages forests, lakes, and stone buildings.
flashcards.example: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid). Limestone buildings dissolve: CaCO₃ + acid → Ca²⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O.

flashcards.definition: Total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an individual, organisation, event, or product.
flashcards.example: Flying one tonne of CO₂. Eating less meat has a lower carbon footprint.

flashcards.definition: Device in car exhausts using platinum/palladium/rhodium catalysts to convert harmful gases: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
flashcards.example: Catalytic converters have dramatically reduced NOₓ and CO emissions from vehicles.

flashcards.definition: Water safe to drink — contains dissolved minerals, very low levels of microbes. NOT the same as chemically pure water.
flashcards.example: Tap water is potable. Pure (distilled) water tastes flat — it lacks minerals.

flashcards.definition: Desalination method: high pressure forces water through a semipermeable membrane, leaving dissolved salts behind.
flashcards.example: Used in Middle Eastern countries to produce fresh water from seawater — energy-intensive.

flashcards.definition: Complete (plentiful O₂): fuel → CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete (limited O₂): fuel → CO (toxic) + C (soot) + H₂O.
flashcards.example: A blue Bunsen flame (complete combustion) vs a yellow flickering flame (incomplete — produces soot).

flashcards.definition: A natural reservoir that absorbs and stores more CO₂ than it releases — oceans, forests, and peat bogs are major carbon sinks.
flashcards.example: The Amazon rainforest absorbs ~2 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year. Deforestation turns sinks into sources.

questions.stem: Granite has large visible crystals. What does this indicate about its formation?
choices: It cooled quickly at Earth's surface
It cooled slowly underground (intrusive), giving crystals time to grow
It was changed by heat and pressure
questions.explanation: Large crystals = slow cooling (intrusive igneous). Magma cooled deep underground over thousands of years, allowing crystals to grow large.

questions.stem: Which rock type is most likely to contain fossils?
choices: Sedimentary — fossils are preserved when organisms are buried in sediment before they decay
questions.explanation: Fossils form when organisms are quickly buried in sediment. Igneous rocks form from molten material (too hot for fossils). Metamorphic rocks' heat/pressure destroy most fossils.

questions.stem: Earth's early atmosphere contained almost no oxygen. What produced the oxygen?
choices: Photosynthesis by early algae and cyanobacteria → O₂ gradually accumulated over billions of years
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Over ~2 billion years, photosynthetic organisms transformed the atmosphere from anoxic to oxygen-rich.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect?
choices: The natural effect is essential for life; the enhanced effect is caused by human emissions adding extra greenhouse gases, trapping more heat
The natural effect is harmful; the enhanced is beneficial
One occurs in winter, the other in summer
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable. The enhanced effect (human-caused) is warming Earth beyond historical norms — the problem is the RATE and MAGNITUDE.

questions.stem: Which gas is produced during INCOMPLETE combustion of hydrocarbons and is toxic to humans?
choices: Carbon monoxide (CO) — binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport
questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion (insufficient O₂) produces CO. CO is colourless, odourless, and deadly — it binds irreversibly to haemoglobin 200× more strongly than O₂.

questions.stem: Which process produces sulfur dioxide, a cause of acid rain?
choices: Burning fossil fuels containing sulfur impurities (coal, some oils)
Both burning fossil fuels and volcanic eruptions — both are significant sources
questions.explanation: Both volcanic eruptions (natural) and burning sulfur-containing fossil fuels (anthropogenic) produce SO₂ — they are the two main sources. Photosynthesis and decomposition do NOT produce SO₂.

questions.stem: How does limestone (CaCO₃) formation in oceans act as a long-term carbon sink?
choices: Limestone absorbs CO₂ from the atmosphere directly
Marine organisms use dissolved CO₂ to build CaCO₃ shells; when they die, shells sink and form limestone — locking carbon away for millions of years
Limestone reacts with CO₂ to form water
questions.explanation: Ocean organisms extract dissolved CO₂ (as carbonate ions) to build shells. Sedimentation of dead organisms forms carbonate rocks — carbon is removed from the short-term cycle.

questions.stem: A catalytic converter changes CO and NO into:
questions.explanation: Catalytic converters reduce toxic CO (to CO₂) and NO (to N₂). Platinum and rhodium catalysts enable this reaction at exhaust temperatures.

questions.stem: Why is desalination not widely used for water supply despite abundant seawater?
choices: Seawater has no salt to remove
Desalination (distillation or reverse osmosis) is extremely energy-intensive and expensive — only viable where energy is cheap and water is scarce
Desalination produces oxygen as a by-product
questions.explanation: Desalination requires enormous amounts of energy to overcome osmotic pressure or boil water. The high cost limits it to wealthy arid regions (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Israel, California).

questions.stem: What is the MAIN reason for increased atmospheric CO₂ since the Industrial Revolution?
choices: Burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and deforestation
questions.explanation: Fossil fuel combustion releases ancient stored carbon as CO₂. Deforestation reduces the biosphere's capacity to absorb CO₂. Together, these drive rising CO₂.

questions.stem: Methane (CH₄) is a more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ but less abundant. A major source is:
choices: Agriculture — cattle digestion (enteric fermentation) and rice paddies produce large amounts of methane
questions.explanation: Livestock (especially cattle) produce methane through gut bacteria. Rice paddies (flooded fields) also produce methane from anaerobic decomposition. Methane traps ~25× more heat per molecule than CO₂.

questions.stem: Marble is a metamorphic rock. What was the parent rock?
choices: Limestone (CaCO₃) → marble — heat and pressure recrystallise the calcite
questions.explanation: Marble is metamorphosed limestone. The heat and pressure recrystallise the calcium carbonate, producing the characteristic interlocking crystal structure and veining.

questions.stem: Why is the ozone layer important for life on Earth?
choices: It absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun, preventing DNA damage and skin cancer
It traps heat to keep Earth warm
questions.explanation: Ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere absorbs UV-B and UV-C radiation. Without it, surface UV levels would be lethal to most life forms. The ozone layer is recovering thanks to the Montreal Protocol.

questions.stem: A city wants to reduce its carbon footprint. Which action would be MOST effective?
choices: Investing in renewable energy (solar, wind) and public transport to replace fossil fuel use
questions.explanation: Energy and transport are the largest CO₂ sources. Switching to renewables eliminates emissions at source. Trees absorb CO₂ (cutting them down increases footprint). Landfills produce methane.

questions.stem: Limestone (CaCO₃) is heated strongly → CaO + CO₂. The CO₂ was originally removed from the ancient atmosphere by:
choices: Marine organisms (using CO₂ to build shells) — their remains formed limestone millions of years ago
questions.explanation: Limestone is ancient sequestered CO₂. Marine organisms incorporated dissolved CO₂ into CaCO₃ shells. Over geological time, these became limestone. Heating releases that ancient carbon back as CO₂.
